A price is one number. What you actually want is the whole distribution around it.

This runs the full chain on a series whose true volatility path is known, so every estimator can be scored against the right answer rather than against a plausible story. 2 599 trading days. The series ends in a volatility spike, which is the case worth getting right.

1Price → returns

Leave the price level behind on the first line

Everything downstream operates on r_t = ln(P_t / P_{t−1}). Prices are non-stationary and their increments scale with level; log returns are additive across time and roughly stationary, which is what makes every variance formula below legal.

For a 20-day window, use the zero-mean form √(Σr²/n) rather than the sample standard deviation. Over 20 days the sample mean is pure noise, and subtracting it costs you a degree of freedom for nothing. On this series that's a small but free improvement: RMSE 4.76 → 4.72 pp.

On real commodity futures there is a step before this one: never take a return across a roll date. The gap between contract months is not a return, and including it injects volatility that never happened.

2Measuring σ

Four estimates of the same hidden quantity

Volatility is never observed. It is inferred, and the inference is noisier than most people assume: the relative standard error of a 20-day estimate is 1/√(2n) ≈ 15.8%. A reading of 38% is really 38% ± 6. A large share of the "volatility spikes" people react to are sampling noise.

This corrects something I told you earlier

I said Yang–Zhang buys roughly 5–7× efficiency and that it was the single cheapest upgrade in the chain. Measured here, that is wrong twice over.

In a controlled experiment under textbook conditions — constant volatility, pure GBM — the gain is 1.73× in RMSE (about 3× in variance terms), not 5–7×. The textbook figure assumes no overnight gap; once 35% of daily variance arrives as a gap, Yang–Zhang estimates that portion with an ordinary variance and the advantage is capped. Discrete sampling also biases the observed high–low range downward by about 1.7 pp.

More importantly, the ranking depends entirely on which target you score against — see step 3.

3The target

A better estimator of the wrong target is still wrong

A 20-day window estimates the 20-day average of volatility. What you need for a forecast is volatility today. When volatility moves fast, those two quantities are far apart, and the gap between them swamps any efficiency difference between estimators.

This is why the real jump in accuracy comes from how observations are weighted, not from which range estimator you pick. Equal weights over a fixed window are the problem; exponential weights are the fix.

estimator of σ todayRMSE vs true σtrelative
20d close-to-close4.72 pp1.0×
20d Yang–Zhang5.07 pp0.9×
EWMA, λ = 0.943.74 pp1.3×
GJR-t filtered0.67 pp7.0×

The GARCH figure is flattering — it is in-sample, and the data were generated by a GARCH process, so this is close to a best case. The ordering, though, is the well-documented one, and it reverses the priority I gave you: exponential filtering first, range estimators second.

4Diagnose

Check that a volatility model is warranted before fitting one

Two autocorrelation functions decide this. Returns should show nothing; squared returns should show slow decay over many lags. If the second one is flat, there is no clustering to model and GARCH will just add parameters.

Then check the shape of the innovations. Excess kurtosis here is 11.9 against 0 for a normal — a "6σ" event under normality is not remotely a 6σ event in this data.

5Fit

Let the information criterion choose the specification

h_t = ω + (α + γ·1[r_{t−1} < 0])·r²_{t−1} + β·h_{t−1}, r_t = √h_t · ε_t, ε_t ~ t(ν)
specificationlog-likelihoodBIC
GARCH(1,1) normal−4 798.79 628.9
GARCH(1,1) t−4 673.49 386.2
GJR(1,1,1) t−4 666.29 379.5
GJR(1,1,1) skew-t−4 664.59 384.0

Fat tails buy 243 BIC points; the leverage term buys 7 more; explicit skewness is rejected. Note the asymmetry sign is an empirical question, not a constant — equities typically show higher volatility after down moves, while energy and agricultural markets often spike on upside supply shocks. Do not import the equity sign into a commodity model.

The two numbers you most want are the two least identified

Every structural parameter is recovered to within 10% on ten years of daily data. But persistence lands 0.6% high, and because both derived quantities divide by 1 − p, that 0.6% becomes a 15% error in the long-run level and a 42% error in the half-life.

Treat σ∞ and the half-life as order-of-magnitude quantities. "Shocks decay over weeks, not days" is supportable. "The half-life is 48.6 days" is not.

6Aggregate

The spike decays, so √T scaling of today's volatility overstates the horizon

E[h_{t+h}] = h∞ + p^{h−1}·(h_{t+1} − h∞) σ²(t,H) = Σ_{h=1..H} E[h_{t+h}]

This single formula is the answer to "I see a volatility spike, now what". Today's conditional volatility is 46.0% against a long-run 28%. Holding 46% flat across 60 days assumes the spike never subsides — which the model, and the data, say it does.

Events the model cannot see

GARCH extrapolates from past returns and knows nothing about the calendar. Scheduled events are added to the variance budget by hand:

σ²_total = σ²_diffusive + n_events · σ²_event

Two events at a typical 4.5% absolute move — implying σ_event ≈ 5.6% — take the 60-day σ from 19.8% to 21.4%, an 7.8% uplift. This is exactly what the options market does mechanically, which is why implied volatility rises into an event and collapses immediately after it.

7Drift

Admit that drift is unknowable, then notice it barely matters

value
μ estimated, 10.3 years1.5% p.a.
95% confidence interval−15.6% to +18.6%
true μ6.0% p.a.
contribution over 60 days0.36%
σ over the same 60 days19.83%

Ten years of data cannot distinguish a 1.5% drift from a 6% one, or from a −10% one. The standard error of the mean is σ/√years, so halving it requires quadrupling your history. You would need centuries.

The saving grace is the scale mismatch: over 60 days the drift contributes 0.36% against a 19.83% standard deviation — a 55:1 ratio. Below roughly one year, set the drift to zero or the risk-free rate and put your effort into the second moment, where the estimation actually converges.

8Simulate

Simulate, because the aggregate has no closed form

Summing GARCH returns over 60 days gives no analytic distribution, and path-dependent questions have none either. 50 000 simulated paths answer both at once.

P(within ±10%)45.6%—

The upside probabilities agree almost exactly; the downside differs by 10.6 points. Two assumptions that look similar in the body of the distribution disagree sharply where the money is. And the last two rows have no closed form at all — a touch probability is roughly twice the terminal probability of the same level, which is the gap between a stop being hit and a position finishing underwater.

9Validate

None of it counts until the intervals are backtested

Every window below is disjoint, so the breach tests are valid. Kupiec tests whether the breach rate matches the nominal rate; Christoffersen tests whether breaches arrive independently, since a model that is too slow produces breaches in clusters.

Read the two tables together — the second one is a warning about backtesting itself

At 20 days there are only 92 disjoint windows. The naive method undercovers by 5 points and the test still cannot reject it (p = 0.118). At 5 days, 369 windows are enough and the same method is rejected at p = 0.044. Nothing about the method changed; only the sample size did.

Ten years of daily data buys you fewer than a hundred independent 20-day observations. If you intend to validate a 20-day interval model, plan for that, and lean on the 50% interval: breaches are five times more frequent, so it converges roughly five times faster. Note that the independence test rejects on the 50% intervals for both methods — breaches still cluster, meaning even the GARCH model adapts more slowly than the data moves.

One more asymmetry worth noting: simulating with t innovations produced worse coverage than aggregating the variance and using normal quantiles. Over 5–20 days, the sum of fat-tailed daily innovations is pulled back toward normality by the central limit theorem faster than the GARCH feedback fattens it. Fat tails matter enormously at the 1-day horizon and much less at the 20-day one.

What this does not do

It produces a distribution, not an edge. The market publishes its own version of this object continuously through the option chain, and the implied distribution is forward-looking where everything above is backward-looking. A position only has positive expected value where your distribution differs from the implied one and you can say why.

The series here is simulated from a known GJR-GARCH process, because this sandbox has no market-data access and because ground truth is what makes the validation meaningful. Everything in the pipeline runs unchanged on real OHLC data; the parameter values will differ, and the GARCH advantage in step 3 will be smaller when the true process is not itself GARCH.

I'm not a financial advisor, and none of this says whether any particular position is worth taking. It is the measurement layer that a decision would need to sit on top of.
